lessons.title: Vertebral Column and Spinal Cord
body: The vertebral column has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 3 to 5 fused coccygeal vertebrae. A typical vertebra has a body anteriorly, a vertebral arch posteriorly (pedicles and laminae), a spinous process, two transverse processes and articular processes that form the zygapophyseal joints. Regional features help identification: cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina that transmit the vertebral artery (usually from C6 upward); thoracic vertebrae have costal facets for the ribs; lumbar vertebrae have large bodies and no foramina or facets. The atlas (C1) has no body and carries the skull; the axis (C2) has the dens, held against the atlas by the transverse ligament, whose rupture risks cord compression.

Intervertebral discs have a gelatinous nucleus pulposus inside a fibrous annulus fibrosus. Herniation most often occurs posterolaterally, where the annulus is thinner and the posterior longitudinal ligament is weaker. Because spinal nerves exit through the intervertebral foramen above the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra in the lumbar region, a posterolateral herniation at L4-L5 typically compresses the traversing L5 root, not the exiting L4 root. A worked example: a patient with L5 radiculopathy has weak great-toe extension and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot.

The spinal cord is shorter than the canal because the column grows faster than the cord during development. In adults the cord ends as the conus medullaris at about the L1-L2 level, and below it lies the cauda equina, a bundle of lumbar and sacral roots in a sac of cerebrospinal fluid. The meninges are the pia mater (adherent to the cord), the arachnoid and the tough dura mater. The subarachnoid space ends at about S2, and the filum terminale extends to the coccyx. Lumbar puncture is done below the conus, usually L3-L4 or L4-L5; the line between the iliac crests (the supracristal plane) crosses roughly L4. The needle passes skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, the epidural space, dura and arachnoid. Epidural anaesthesia stops just short of the dura.

The cord has cervical and lumbosacral enlargements for the limb plexuses. Spinal nerves number 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal. There are eight cervical nerves but seven cervical vertebrae, because C1 to C7 exit above their vertebrae and C8 exits below C7. From T1 downward each nerve exits below the vertebra of the same number, which is why the cauda equina roots descend a long way before leaving.

lessons.title: Cord Tracts, Blood Supply and Lesions
body: Three ascending systems matter clinically. The dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry fine touch, vibration and proprioception ipsilaterally and cross in the medulla. The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature from the contralateral body, because its fibres synapse in the dorsal horn and cross within one or two segments through the anterior white commissure. The spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception to the cerebellum. The main descending pathway is the lateral corticospinal tract, which crosses at the pyramidal decussation in the medulla, so it controls ipsilateral muscles below the level of a cord lesion.

A cord hemisection produces Brown-Sequard syndrome. Below the lesion there is ipsilateral weakness (corticospinal), ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception (dorsal column) and contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic). At the level of the lesion there is ipsilateral segmental loss of all sensation and lower motor neuron weakness. Syringomyelia, a central cavity usually in the cervical cord, interrupts the crossing spinothalamic fibres in the anterior commissure and gives a cape-like bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch, a dissociated sensory loss.

Blood supply comes from one anterior spinal artery and two posterior spinal arteries, reinforced by radicular arteries. The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two thirds of the cord, including corticospinal tracts and spinothalamic tracts. Occlusion produces motor paralysis and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion but spares the dorsal columns, which the posterior spinal arteries supply. The great anterior radicular artery of Adamkiewicz, usually arising on the left from a lower thoracic or upper lumbar intercostal or lumbar artery, feeds the lower cord. It is endangered during aortic aneurysm surgery, and injury can produce paraplegia.

Level matters. Upper motor neuron lesions cause spasticity, hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response; lower motor neuron lesions cause flaccid weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and hyporeflexia. Cauda equina syndrome from a large central disc herniation causes saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention or overflow incontinence and variable leg weakness, and is a surgical emergency. Remember that the conus and cauda equina are different structures: conus lesions tend to be early and bilateral with more sphincter involvement, while cauda equina lesions are asymmetric root lesions. Spinal cord compression from a vertebral metastasis or abscess is likewise an emergency, because the level of the sensory deficit helps localise the lesion to the segment just above it.

lessons.title: Thoracic Wall, Pleura and Lungs
body: The thoracic cage consists of 12 pairs of ribs, the thoracic vertebrae and the sternum. Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs attaching directly to the sternum by costal cartilage, ribs 8 to 10 attach via the cartilage above, and ribs 11 and 12 are floating. Each intercostal space contains three muscle layers (external, internal and innermost intercostals) and a neurovascular bundle running in the plane between the internal and innermost layers in the order vein, artery, nerve from superior to inferior (VAN). The bundle lies in the costal groove along the lower border of the rib above. Therefore a chest tube or needle thoracostomy is placed just above the upper border of the rib below, to avoid damaging it.

Each lung is covered by visceral pleura, which is insensitive to pain and is supplied by the autonomic nervous system. The parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum and is sensitive to pain via the intercostal nerves and the phrenic nerve. The pleural cavity ends in costodiaphragmatic recesses, the lowest points where fluid collects, reaching rib 8 in the midclavicular line, rib 10 in the midaxillary line and rib 12 posteriorly. Pleural effusion is therefore tapped posteriorly, low in the space but above the diaphragm. A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space; a tension pneumothorax acts as a one-way valve, shifting the mediastinum, compressing the great veins and causing hypotension.

The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, lower) and two fissures; the left has two lobes with an oblique fissure and a lingula, the homologue of the middle lobe, plus a cardiac notch. The right main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left, so aspirated material and foreign bodies more often enter the right lung, usually the posterior segment of the right upper lobe when supine or the superior segment of the lower lobe. Each lobe divides into bronchopulmonary segments, each with its own segmental bronchus and pulmonary artery branch, and separated by connective tissue; this allows a segment to be surgically resected. The pulmonary veins lie between segments.

The diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5), which keeps the diaphragm alive. Irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura refers pain to the shoulder tip, because the phrenic and supraclavicular nerves share the C3 to C5 dermatomes. The lymphatic drainage of the lung passes to hilar and tracheobronchial nodes.

lessons.title: The Heart and Mediastinum
body: The mediastinum is the central compartment between the pleural cavities. It is divided at the sternal angle (T4-T5 level) into a superior part and an inferior part; the inferior part is split into anterior, middle (containing the heart and pericardium) and posterior portions. The thymus lies in the anterior and superior mediastinum; the oesophagus, thoracic aorta, thoracic duct, azygos system and sympathetic trunks lie posteriorly. The sternal angle also marks the second costal cartilage, the start and end of the aortic arch and the carina bifurcation.

The heart sits in a fibrous pericardium lined by the serous parietal pericardium; the visceral layer (epicardium) covers the heart, with the pericardial cavity between. Rapid accumulation of fluid in this cavity compresses the heart: cardiac tamponade produces hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins (Beck triad). The right atrium receives the venae cavae and coronary sinus, the right ventricle sends blood to the pulmonary trunk, the left atrium receives four pulmonary veins and the left ventricle pumps to the aorta. Anteriorly, the sternocostal surface is mostly right ventricle; the left atrium forms most of the base posteriorly, and lies against the oesophagus, so enlargement can compress it.

The right coronary artery (RCA) arises from the right aortic sinus and supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, the SA node in most people and, in a right-dominant circulation (about 80 percent), gives rise to the posterior descending artery that supplies the inferior septum and AV node. The left coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus and divides into the left anterior descending (LAD), which supplies the anterior left ventricle and the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum, and the circumflex, which supplies the lateral and posterior left ventricle. LAD occlusion causes an anterior infarct; RCA occlusion may cause an inferior infarct with bradycardia or AV block because of nodal ischaemia.

The conduction system comprises the SA node at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium, the AV node in the triangle of Koch, the bundle of His and the left and right bundle branches. Sympathetic fibres from T1-T4 accelerate the heart, and the vagus slows it. Visceral cardiac pain travels with sympathetic afferents to T1-T4, so angina is felt in the chest and medial arm and sometimes the jaw. The heart valves auscultate at the sites downstream of flow: aortic at the right second intercostal space, pulmonary at the left second, tricuspid at the left lower sternal border and mitral at the apex in the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

lessons.title: Abdominal Wall, Inguinal Canal and Hernias
body: The anterolateral abdominal wall has, from superficial to deep, skin, Camper fascia (fatty), Scarpa fascia (membranous), the external oblique, internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat and parietal peritoneum. The rectus abdominis lies in the rectus sheath; above the arcuate line the sheath splits around it, and below the line all aponeuroses pass anterior to the muscle, leaving only transversalis fascia behind. Dermatome T10 is at the umbilicus; the nerves are the lower intercostal, subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.

The inguinal canal is an oblique passage about 4 cm long above the inguinal ligament, running from the deep ring (an opening in the transversalis fascia) to the superficial ring (an opening in the external oblique aponeurosis). In men it carries the spermatic cord; in women, the round ligament of the uterus. Both sexes have the ilioinguinal nerve in the canal. The roof is the internal oblique and transversus abdominis (the conjoint tendon forms the posterior wall medially), the anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis, the floor is the inguinal ligament, and the posterior wall is transversalis fascia. The spermatic cord layers derive from the abdominal wall: external spermatic fascia from the external oblique, cremasteric muscle and fascia from the internal oblique, and internal spermatic fascia from transversalis fascia.

Hernias are protrusions through a weakness. Hesselbach triangle is bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, the rectus sheath medially and the inguinal ligament below. A direct inguinal hernia passes through this triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, pushes through the posterior wall of the canal and usually comes through the superficial ring only. An indirect inguinal hernia passes through the deep ring lateral to the epigastric vessels, follows the course of the cord inside the internal spermatic fascia, and is often congenital, from a patent processus vaginalis. Femoral hernias go below and lateral to the pubic tubercle through the femoral ring, medial to the femoral vein, and carry a high risk of strangulation because the ring is narrow and rigid. Femoral hernias are commoner in women.

The key distinction is the relationship to the inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery. A worked example: an elderly man with a bulge appearing on straining, reducing when lying, medial to the epigastric vessels at surgery, has a direct hernia. A young child with a bulge descending to the scrotum has an indirect hernia.

lessons.title: Peritoneum and the GI Viscera
body: The peritoneum is a serous membrane. The parietal layer lines the cavity and is pain sensitive through somatic nerves; the visceral layer covers organs and is sensitive to stretch via visceral afferents. Organs are intraperitoneal (wrapped, with a mesentery, such as the stomach, jejunum, ileum, liver and spleen), primarily retroperitoneal (behind the peritoneum, such as the kidneys, adrenals and aorta) or secondarily retroperitoneal (they started intraperitoneal, then fused to the posterior wall, such as the duodenum except its first part, ascending and descending colon, and pancreas except the tail). A helpful mnemonic is SAD PUCKER. The lesser omentum runs from the liver to the lesser curvature and first part of the duodenum; its free edge, the hepatoduodenal ligament, contains the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery proper, bile duct). The opening posterior to it is the epiploic foramen, the entrance to the lesser sac; the Pringle manoeuvre compresses the free edge to control liver bleeding. The greater omentum hangs from the greater curvature.

The foregut gives the oesophagus to the second part of the duodenum (above the major duodenal papilla), plus liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen, and is supplied by the coeliac trunk (T12). The midgut runs from the duodenum below the papilla to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon and is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (SMA; L1). The hindgut runs from the distal third of the transverse colon to the upper anal canal and is supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA; L3). Pain follows embryologic origin: foregut disease is felt in the epigastrium, midgut in the periumbilical region and hindgut in the suprapubic region. Appendicitis classically starts periumbilical (midgut visceral pain, T10) and migrates to the right lower quadrant once the parietal peritoneum is irritated, at McBurney point about one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.

The stomach has lesser and greater curvatures, cardia, fundus, body and pylorus. Its blood supply runs along both curvatures: the left and right gastric arteries along the lesser, and the left and right gastroepiploic arteries along the greater, with short gastric arteries to the fundus. The posterior duodenal ulcer can erode the gastroduodenal artery and bleed severely, while an anterior ulcer is more likely to perforate into the peritoneal cavity. The vagus nerves provide parasympathetic innervation: anterior vagal trunk from the left vagus, posterior from the right.

The small bowel is distinguished by the jejunum having long vasa recta and prominent plicae, and the ileum having shorter vasa recta and Peyer patches. Meckel diverticulum is a remnant of the vitelline duct in about 2 percent of people, about 2 feet (60 cm) from the ileocaecal valve, and may contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue. The colon has taeniae coli, haustra and epiploic appendages.

lessons.title: Abdominal Vasculature and Portal Anastomoses
body: The abdominal aorta begins at the aortic hiatus (T12) and ends by bifurcating at L4. Its unpaired ventral branches are the coeliac trunk (T12), SMA (L1) and IMA (L3). The coeliac trunk gives the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries; the common hepatic gives the gastroduodenal artery and hepatic artery proper, and the gastroduodenal divides into the superior pancreaticoduodenal and right gastroepiploic arteries. The paired lateral branches are the inferior phrenic, middle suprarenal, renal and gonadal arteries; lumbar arteries arise posteriorly, and the median sacral artery from the bifurcation. The SMA supplies the pancreatic head and duodenum (via the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery), jejunum, ileum and colon to the splenic flexure region. The marginal artery of Drummond connects the SMA and IMA territories, and watershed zones near the splenic flexure are vulnerable to ischaemia in hypotension.

The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; the inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic. It carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut to the liver sinusoids, and the hepatic veins drain into the inferior vena cava. In portal hypertension, blood seeks a path around the liver through portosystemic anastomoses where portal and systemic veins meet. At the lower oesophagus, left gastric veins (portal) meet oesophageal veins draining to the azygos (systemic), producing oesophageal varices with risk of haematemesis. At the umbilicus, paraumbilical veins (portal) join epigastric veins, producing caput medusae. At the anorectal junction, the superior rectal vein (portal via the IMV) meets the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic via the internal iliac and pudendal), producing rectal varices, distinct from haemorrhoids. Retroperitoneal anastomoses also exist between colonic veins and the posterior abdominal wall.

The inferior vena cava forms at L5 from the common iliac veins and ascends on the right of the aorta, passing through the diaphragm at T8. It receives the right gonadal vein directly, while the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein. This arrangement explains why varicoceles occur more often on the left, because the left testicular vein enters at a right angle and the left renal vein can be compressed between the SMA and aorta (the nutcracker phenomenon). An abrupt left-sided varicocele that does not decompress when lying down can signal a renal mass obstructing the left renal vein.

The SMA has an important anatomical relationship with the third part of the duodenum, which passes between the SMA and aorta. Loss of retroperitoneal fat in rapid weight loss can narrow this angle and compress the duodenum, producing SMA syndrome with postprandial vomiting. Acute mesenteric ischaemia from an SMA embolus produces severe pain out of proportion to examination.

lessons.title: Retroperitoneum, Kidneys and Posterior Wall
body: The retroperitoneum lies behind the parietal peritoneum and contains the kidneys, adrenal glands, ureters, aorta, inferior vena cava, the pancreas (mostly), most of the duodenum, and lymph nodes and nerves. Each kidney sits at about T12 to L3, the right slightly lower because of the liver. The kidney has a fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, the renal (Gerota) fascia and pararenal fat. The renal hilum from anterior to posterior contains the vein, artery and pelvis (the order VAP). Segmental arteries are end arteries, so occlusion causes segmental infarction. The renal arteries arise at L1-L2; the left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta below the SMA origin, and the right renal artery passes posterior to the IVC.

The ureters descend on the psoas major, cross the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery and pass to the bladder. They have three physiological narrowings, where stones tend to lodge: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim, and the vesicoureteric junction, the narrowest. Renal colic radiates from loin to groin because the ureter is supplied by T10-L2 segments, which share the ilioinguinal and genitofemoral dermatomes with the scrotum or labia. Surgical caution: in the pelvis the ureter lies under the uterine artery in women ("water under the bridge") and under the vas deferens in men, so ligation of those vessels can injure the ureter.

The adrenal glands lie above the kidneys. The right adrenal vein is short and drains directly to the IVC; the left drains into the left renal vein. The cortex has three zones (glomerulosa makes aldosterone, fasciculata cortisol, reticularis androgens) and the medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion producing catecholamines; its preganglionic sympathetic supply is unusual in having no postsynaptic neurons. The pancreas has head, neck, body and tail; the head sits in the duodenal C-loop, with the uncinate process behind the SMV, and the tail lies in the splenorenal ligament near the splenic hilum. Pancreatic head cancer may compress the common bile duct, causing painless jaundice.

The posterior abdominal wall contains psoas major (hip flexor, from lumbar vertebrae and discs to the lesser trochanter), iliacus and quadratus lumborum. The psoas lies near the ureter and sympathetic trunk; a psoas abscess or irritation produces pain on hip extension. The lumbar plexus forms within psoas from L1-L4 and gives the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral and obturator nerves. The femoral nerve emerges on the lateral border of psoas, while the obturator emerges from the medial border.

lessons.title: Pelvis and Pelvic Viscera
body: The bony pelvis is formed by the two hip bones (each fusing ilium, ischium and pubis at the acetabulum), the sacrum and coccyx. The pelvic brim (pelvic inlet) separates the false pelvis above from the true pelvis below. In females the inlet is wider and rounder and the subpubic angle is larger, which suits childbirth. The pelvic floor is formed by the levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus) and coccygeus, covered by fascia. The puborectalis forms a sling that maintains the anorectal angle, a major mechanism of faecal continence. The levator ani is innervated by nerves from S3-S4 and the pudendal nerve, and weakening after childbirth contributes to pelvic organ prolapse.

The bladder in adults lies behind the pubic symphysis; when full it rises above the pubis and the peritoneum is lifted off the anterior wall, allowing suprapubic needle aspiration without entering the peritoneal cavity. The ureters enter the bladder posteriorly at the trigone, which is smooth muscle, whereas the rest of the wall is detrusor muscle. In males the prostate surrounds the urethra just below the bladder. Its posterior surface lies against the rectum, which is why digital rectal examination assesses it, and the peripheral zone is where most carcinomas arise, whereas benign enlargement of the transition zone compresses the urethra and causes obstructive urinary symptoms. The seminal vesicles lie behind the bladder, and the vas deferens passes superior to the ureter near the bladder.

In females the uterus lies between the bladder and the rectum, usually anteverted and anteflexed. The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold supporting the uterus, tubes and ovaries. The round ligament runs through the inguinal canal to the labia majora; the ovarian ligament connects ovary to uterus; the suspensory ligament of the ovary carries the ovarian vessels. The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligaments are the main support of the cervix and carry the uterine vessels, with the ureter lying nearby. The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity, and pus or blood may collect there; it can be drained through the posterior vaginal fornix. The male equivalent is the rectovesical pouch.

Arterial supply to the pelvis is mostly the internal iliac artery. Its anterior division gives the uterine, vaginal, vesical, middle rectal, obturator and internal pudendal arteries, and its posterior division gives the iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal arteries. The ovarian artery comes from the aorta, and the superior rectal from the inferior mesenteric. Lymph drains from most pelvic organs to the internal and external iliac nodes, but the ovary and testis drain to para-aortic nodes, and the superficial perineum and lower vagina to the superficial inguinal nodes. Parasympathetic fibres from S2-S4 (pelvic splanchnic nerves) cause bladder contraction and erection, while sympathetic fibres supply emission and ejaculation.

lessons.title: The Perineum
body: The perineum is the diamond-shaped region below the pelvic floor, bounded by the pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx. A line between the ischial tuberosities divides it into the anterior urogenital triangle and the posterior anal triangle. The urogenital triangle contains the superficial and deep perineal pouches. The superficial pouch has the ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus and superficial transverse perineal muscles, plus the erectile tissues (the crura and bulb of the penis or clitoris and vestibular bulbs). The deep pouch contains the external urethral sphincter and deep transverse perineal muscle. The perineal body, a central tendinous point, anchors many of these muscles and is torn in obstetric injury; an episiotomy cuts near it.

The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) is the main nerve of the perineum. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, passes around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament and re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen, then travels in the pudendal canal with the internal pudendal vessels. It gives the inferior rectal nerve, perineal nerve and dorsal nerve of penis or clitoris, supplying the external anal sphincter, perineal skin and muscles, and sensation of the genitalia. For a pudendal nerve block during childbirth, the clinician palpates the ischial spine transvaginally and injects near the nerve as it passes it, so the spine is the key landmark. The bulbourethral glands lie in the deep pouch.

The anal canal is about 4 cm long. The pectinate (dentate) line marks the junction of endoderm (hindgut) and ectoderm. Above the line, blood comes from the superior rectal artery, drains to the portal system through the superior rectal vein and lymph to the internal iliac nodes, and the mucosa has visceral innervation, so it is insensitive to cutting and pinprick. Below the line, supply is by the inferior rectal artery, drainage to systemic veins, lymph to superficial inguinal nodes and sensation by the somatic inferior rectal nerve, so lesions here are painful. Internal haemorrhoids arise above the line and are usually painless bleeding; external haemorrhoids below it are painful. Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal below the line spreads to inguinal nodes, while rectal adenocarcinoma spreads to iliac and mesenteric nodes.

The ischioanal (ischiorectal) fossae are fat-filled wedges lateral to the anal canal that allow it to distend. Abscesses can spread between the two fossae through the deep postanal space, producing a horseshoe pattern. The internal anal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle with sympathetic and parasympathetic supply, while the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.

lessons.title: Gluteal Region, Thigh and Hip
body: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket synovial joint between the femoral head and the acetabulum. Stability comes from the deep socket, labrum and strong capsular ligaments (iliofemoral, pubofemoral, ischiofemoral). Blood supply to the femoral head comes mainly from the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, branches of the profunda femoris, forming a ring at the base of the neck, with a small contribution from the artery of the ligament of the head. Femoral neck fractures can disrupt the retinacular vessels and cause avascular necrosis of the head, especially in older patients. Typical signs of a displaced neck-of-femur fracture are a shortened, externally rotated leg.

In the gluteal region the gluteus maximus extends and externally rotates the thigh, innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5-S2). The gluteus medius and minimus abduct the thigh and keep the pelvis level when standing on one leg; they are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). Damage to the superior gluteal nerve produces a Trendelenburg gait: when standing on the affected leg, the pelvis drops on the opposite side. Intramuscular injections are given in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve, which leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. The sciatic nerve (L4-S3) has tibial and common fibular components, and in the posterior thigh it supplies the hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris) and the hamstring part of adductor magnus.

The femoral triangle is bordered by the inguinal ligament, sartorius and adductor longus. Its contents from lateral to medial are the femoral nerve, artery, vein and the femoral canal with lymphatics (NAVEL: nerve, artery, vein, empty space, lymphatics). The femoral sheath encloses the artery, vein and canal but not the nerve. The femoral pulse is felt at the midinguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis, and the femoral vein is medial to the artery, a point that matters for central venous cannulation. The femoral nerve (L2-L4) supplies the anterior compartment: quadriceps femoris (knee extension) and sartorius, with the saphenous nerve giving sensation to the medial leg and foot. Femoral nerve injury causes weak knee extension and loss of the patellar reflex.

The medial compartment (adductors, gracilis) is supplied by the obturator nerve (L2-L4), and obturator injury weakens adduction and leaves numbness of the medial thigh. The posterior compartment is the sciatic territory. Deep venous drainage runs with the arteries into the femoral vein, and a superficial great saphenous vein passes anterior to the medial malleolus and joins the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction, which is the source of vein harvests for bypass grafting. The adductor canal carries the femoral vessels and saphenous nerve and ends at the adductor hiatus, where the artery becomes popliteal.

lessons.title: Knee, Leg and Foot
body: The knee is a hinge joint with some rotation, with cruciate and collateral ligaments and menisci. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) prevents anterior translation of the tibia on the femur, and the posterior cruciate (PCL) prevents posterior translation. The medial collateral ligament resists valgus stress and is attached to the medial meniscus, so injury to one often involves the other. The lateral meniscus is more mobile. A pivoting injury with a pop and rapid swelling suggests ACL rupture, and the anterior drawer and Lachman tests are positive. The unhappy triad is classically ACL, MCL and medial meniscus injury, although more recent data suggest lateral meniscus tears are frequent with ACL ruptures.

The popliteal fossa contains from superficial to deep the tibial nerve, popliteal vein and popliteal artery, the artery being deepest and closest to the femur. A supracondylar femur fracture or knee dislocation may injure the artery. The sciatic nerve divides near the apex into the tibial nerve and the common fibular (peroneal) nerve. The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula, where it is superficial and vulnerable to fracture, casts or compression. It divides into the superficial fibular nerve (everts the foot, sensation to the dorsum of the foot) and the deep fibular nerve (dorsiflexion and toe extension, sensation of the first web space). Injury produces foot drop with a high-stepping gait and loss of sensation of the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. The tibial nerve supplies plantarflexors and the muscles of the sole through the medial and lateral plantar nerves, and injury causes loss of plantarflexion and sole sensation.

The leg has anterior, lateral, superficial posterior and deep posterior compartments. The anterior compartment contains the dorsiflexors and the anterior tibial vessels with the deep fibular nerve; the lateral contains the fibularis longus and brevis; the posterior ones contain the gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior and long flexors. Fractures or reperfusion after ischaemia raise pressure within a tight fascial compartment, causing compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense swelling, and later paraesthesia, with pulses often preserved until late. Treatment is surgical fasciotomy. The anterior compartment is the one most often involved.

The foot is supported by medial and lateral longitudinal arches and the transverse arch, held by bones and ligaments including the plantar aponeurosis and the spring ligament. Ankle sprains most commonly involve the lateral ligament complex (the anterior talofibular ligament is the weakest and most frequently torn) during inversion injury, because the deltoid ligament on the medial side is stronger. The dorsalis pedis artery is palpated lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, and the posterior tibial artery pulse behind the medial malleolus. Tarsal tunnel syndrome is entrapment of the tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus.

lessons.title: Shoulder, Axilla and Rotator Cuff
body: The glenohumeral joint is a ball-and-socket joint with the greatest range of motion of any joint, bought at the price of stability. The glenoid is shallow, deepened only slightly by the labrum, so dislocation is common. Anterior-inferior dislocation is most frequent and may injure the axillary nerve, which winds around the surgical neck of the humerus. The rotator cuff comprises supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis (SITS). Together they hold the humeral head in the glenoid. Supraspinatus initiates abduction in the first 15 degrees and is the most commonly torn; infraspinatus and teres minor externally rotate; subscapularis internally rotates. Supraspinatus passes beneath the acromion and can be impinged, causing a painful arc of abduction between about 60 and 120 degrees.

Nerve supply to the scapular muscles: suprascapular nerve (C5-C6) to supraspinatus and infraspinatus, upper and lower subscapular nerves to subscapularis, axillary nerve to teres minor and deltoid. The deltoid abducts from 15 to 90 degrees, and the axillary nerve also supplies a patch of skin over the lateral shoulder (the regimental badge area); loss of that sensation together with deltoid weakness points to axillary nerve injury. Serratus anterior, innervated by the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7), holds the scapula against the chest wall. Injury, for instance during axillary lymph node dissection or mastectomy, causes a winged scapula. Trapezius, supplied by the accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI), elevates the scapula; injury to the nerve in the posterior triangle causes a drooping shoulder and weak shrug.

The axilla is a pyramidal space between the arm and chest wall. Its apex is the cervico-axillary canal, bounded by the clavicle, first rib and scapula; its contents are the axillary artery and vein, the cords and branches of the brachial plexus and lymph nodes in fat. The axillary artery begins at the lateral border of the first rib as the continuation of the subclavian and ends at the inferior border of teres major, becoming the brachial artery. It is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor and gives off the superior thoracic, thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries, then the subscapular, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries. The scapular anastomosis around the scapula provides collateral flow if the subclavian or axillary artery is ligated.

Axillary lymph nodes drain the upper limb, the breast (about 75 percent of lymph from the breast drains to axillary nodes) and the thoracic wall above the umbilicus. Sentinel node biopsy identifies the first node to receive drainage from a breast tumour. The clavicle is the most commonly fractured bone, usually at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds, with the medial fragment pulled up by sternocleidomastoid.

lessons.title: The Brachial Plexus
body: The brachial plexus forms from the anterior rami of C5-T1. Learning its architecture lets a clinician localise any lesion. The five roots form three trunks (upper C5-C6, middle C7, lower C8-T1), each trunk splits into anterior and posterior divisions, and divisions recombine into three cords named for their relationship to the axillary artery: lateral, posterior and medial. The mnemonic is Randy Travis Drinks Cold Beer: roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches. The roots and trunks lie in the posterior triangle of the neck between the scalene muscles, the cords in the axilla.

Branches from the roots include the dorsal scapular nerve (C5, to rhomboids) and long thoracic nerve (C5-C7, to serratus anterior). From the upper trunk comes the suprascapular nerve. The lateral cord gives the lateral pectoral nerve, the musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7) and the lateral root of the median nerve. The medial cord gives the medial pectoral, medial brachial and antebrachial cutaneous nerves, the ulnar nerve (C8-T1) and the medial root of the median nerve. The posterior cord gives the upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves. The median nerve is thus formed by two roots forming an M with the lateral and medial cords on either side of the axillary artery.

Upper trunk injury (Erb-Duchenne palsy, C5-C6) results from excessive widening of the angle between the neck and shoulder, for example when a baby's shoulder is stuck at delivery (shoulder dystocia) or in a fall onto the shoulder. The arm hangs in adduction and internal rotation with the forearm pronated, the waiter's tip position, because abductors, external rotators and biceps are weak. Lower trunk injury (Klumpke palsy, C8-T1) follows traction on an abducted arm, such as grabbing a branch while falling, and affects the intrinsic hand muscles, causing a claw hand; if T1 sympathetic fibres are involved, Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) appears. A cervical rib or a Pancoast tumour at the apex of the lung can also compress the lower trunk and subclavian vessels (thoracic outlet syndrome).

A useful framework for lesions: a lateral cord lesion spares the ulnar nerve but weakens elbow flexion; a posterior cord lesion causes weakness of shoulder abduction and wrist and finger extension (axillary and radial nerves); a medial cord lesion produces a claw hand with sensory loss in the medial arm and hand. Total plexus injuries from motorcycle accidents often avulse roots from the cord; sensory loss with a preserved axon reflex (the histamine flare) suggests a preganglionic lesion because the dorsal root ganglion remains intact.

lessons.title: Arm, Elbow and Nerve Injuries
body: The arm has anterior and posterior compartments separated by intermuscular septa. The anterior compartment (biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis) flexes the elbow and is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7), which pierces coracobrachialis and continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. The posterior compartment (triceps) extends the elbow and is supplied by the radial nerve (C5-T1). The brachial artery runs medially along the arm and, at the cubital fossa, lies medial to the biceps tendon. In the fossa from lateral to medial are the radial nerve (deep), the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve. The median cubital vein crosses the fossa and is used for venepuncture; it lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis, which protects the artery and median nerve.

The radial nerve winds around the humerus in the radial (spiral) groove on the posterior aspect of the humeral shaft, with the profunda brachii artery. A mid-shaft humeral fracture can injure it, causing wrist drop (loss of wrist and finger extension), weakness of supination, loss of sensation over the dorsum of the hand and first web space, and preserved triceps because the branches to triceps leave proximally. Compression in the axilla, such as crutch use, can also affect the triceps. Radial wrist drop must be distinguished from lesions that affect only the posterior interosseous nerve, a deep branch winding around the radial neck, which causes finger drop but no sensory loss and no wrist drop of the full type.

The axillary nerve injury occurs with surgical neck fractures of the humerus. The medial epicondyle fracture injures the ulnar nerve in the groove behind it, giving the funny bone sensation when struck. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow causes numbness of the little finger and the medial ring finger, weakness of the interossei and adductor pollicis (positive Froment sign, in which the patient flexes the thumb interphalangeal joint to hold a paper) and clawing, more marked in lesions at the wrist than at the elbow (the ulnar paradox) because the flexor digitorum profundus to digits 4 and 5 is spared at the wrist and pulls the fingers into flexion.

A supracondylar fracture of the humerus in children can injure the median nerve (particularly the anterior interosseous branch) and the brachial artery, and a resulting forearm compartment ischaemia can produce Volkmann contracture. A worked example: a child with a supracondylar fracture who cannot make an OK sign has anterior interosseous nerve involvement, since the flexor pollicis longus and the lateral flexor digitorum profundus are weak.

lessons.title: Forearm and Hand
body: The forearm has a flexor-pronator anterior compartment, mostly supplied by the median nerve, with flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus supplied by the ulnar nerve, and an extensor-supinator posterior compartment supplied by the radial nerve (through the posterior interosseous nerve). The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres and gives the anterior interosseous nerve, which supplies flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus without a cutaneous branch. The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the carpal tunnel, so the thenar skin sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.

The carpal tunnel is bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament), and transmits the median nerve with nine flexor tendons: four flexor digitorum superficialis, four flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus. Compression of the median nerve causes numbness and tingling in the lateral three and a half digits (palmar side), worse at night, with thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction late in the disease. Tinel and Phalen signs are positive. Causes include repetitive use, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the retinaculum in Guyon canal, and so are not affected by carpal tunnel syndrome.

The thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis) are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, and the first two lumbricals by the median nerve. The remaining intrinsic muscles, including the hypothenar group, all interossei (dorsal abduct, palmar adduct: DAB and PAD), the third and fourth lumbricals and adductor pollicis, are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. The simplest rule is LOAF: the lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis are median. A median nerve lesion at the elbow gives the hand of benediction when making a fist, as the index and middle fingers cannot flex.

The hand has a dual arterial supply: the superficial palmar arch (mostly ulnar artery) and the deep palmar arch (mostly radial artery). The anatomical snuffbox, between the extensor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus tendons, houses the radial artery and the scaphoid. Scaphoid fractures follow a fall on an outstretched hand, cause snuffbox tenderness and may be missed on early radiographs. The scaphoid blood supply enters distally and flows retrograde, so fractures through the waist can cause proximal pole avascular necrosis and nonunion. The Allen test assesses the collateral flow in the hand before radial artery puncture.

lessons.title: Skull, Meninges and Intracranial Haemorrhage
body: The cranial floor has three fossae. The anterior fossa holds the frontal lobes and the cribriform plate, through which olfactory nerve filaments pass; fracture here can cause anosmia and CSF rhinorrhoea. The middle fossa holds the temporal lobes and pituitary fossa and contains the optic canal, superior orbital fissure and the foramina rotundum, ovale and spinosum. The posterior fossa holds the cerebellum and brainstem and the foramen magnum and jugular foramen. Foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3) and the accessory meningeal artery; foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery; foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (V2); the jugular foramen transmits cranial nerves IX, X and XI and the internal jugular vein; and the internal acoustic meatus transmits VII and VIII.

Three meningeal layers cover the brain. The dura mater has an outer periosteal layer and an inner meningeal layer, which separate to form dural venous sinuses. The arachnoid mater lies beneath it, with the subarachnoid space containing CSF and the major arteries and veins. The pia mater adheres to the brain surface. The dura is supplied mainly by the middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, which enters through foramen spinosum and lies on the inner surface of the pterion, a thin H-shaped junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones. A blow to the pterion can tear this artery, causing an epidural haematoma, a lens-shaped (biconvex) collection that does not cross suture lines. Classically there is a brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then deterioration from rising arterial pressure and herniation.

Subdural haematoma, in contrast, results from tearing of bridging veins that cross the subdural space to the dural sinuses; it is crescent-shaped, crosses suture lines and is common in the elderly and alcoholic, where brain atrophy stretches the veins, with a presentation over days to weeks. Subarachnoid haemorrhage commonly follows rupture of a berry aneurysm at the circle of Willis, especially the anterior communicating artery junction, and causes a sudden severe thunderclap headache. Berry aneurysms are associated with polycystic kidney disease.

The dural venous sinuses drain the brain to the internal jugular veins. The superior sagittal sinus runs in the falx cerebri and drains through the confluence of sinuses to the transverse and sigmoid sinuses. The cavernous sinus on either side of the sella turcica contains the internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve (CN VI) within the sinus, and in its lateral wall CN III, IV, V1 and V2. Infection from the dangerous area of the face can spread via the valveless facial and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus, producing thrombosis with ophthalmoplegia, proptosis and sensory loss over the forehead and cheek.

lessons.title: The Cranial Nerves
body: The cranial nerves are I olfactory, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear, V trigeminal, VI abducens, VII facial, VIII vestibulocochlear, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus, XI accessory and XII hypoglossal. I and II attach to the forebrain, III and IV to the midbrain, V to the pons, VI, VII and VIII at the pontomedullary junction, and IX to XII to the medulla (XI has spinal roots too). Function: I, II and VIII are purely sensory; III, IV, VI, XI and XII are purely motor; V, VII, IX and X are mixed. Parasympathetic fibres travel with III (ciliary ganglion; pupil constriction), VII (pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia; lacrimal and salivary glands), IX (otic ganglion; parotid) and X (thoracic and abdominal viscera).

The eye muscles are supplied by three nerves: the lateral rectus by VI, the superior oblique by IV, and the rest by III. The mnemonic is LR6 SO4. A complete oculomotor palsy produces a down-and-out eye (unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique), ptosis from levator palpebrae paralysis and a dilated pupil from loss of parasympathetic fibres, which travel on the outside of the nerve and are compressed first by an expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm or uncal herniation. In diabetic ischaemic third nerve palsy the pupil is often spared, because the central fibres bear the ischaemia and the peripheral parasympathetic fibres are spared. Abducens palsy causes an inability to abduct and horizontal diplopia, a long intracranial course making it a false localising sign in raised intracranial pressure.

The trigeminal nerve divides into V1 (ophthalmic, through the superior orbital fissure), V2 (maxillary, foramen rotundum) and V3 (mandibular, foramen ovale). V3 carries motor fibres to the muscles of mastication. The corneal reflex has sensory limb V1 and motor limb VII. The facial nerve exits through the stylomastoid foramen, supplies muscles of facial expression and runs through the parotid gland; before that it gives chorda tympani (taste to the anterior two thirds of the tongue), the nerve to stapedius and greater petrosal nerve. Lower motor neuron facial palsy (Bell palsy) paralyses the entire half of the face, including the forehead, whereas an upper motor neuron lesion (such as a stroke) spares the forehead because the upper facial nucleus receives bilateral cortical input.

The glossopharyngeal nerve provides taste and sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and the afferent limb of the gag reflex, with the vagus the efferent limb. The vagus supplies the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles; the recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch on the left and the right subclavian artery on the right, and injury causes hoarseness (thyroid surgery risk). The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue muscles, and a lesion makes the tongue deviate toward the side of the lesion because the genioglossus on the intact side pushes it across.

lessons.title: Neck Triangles, Thyroid and Fascial Spaces
body: The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) divides each side of the neck into an anterior triangle and a posterior triangle. The anterior triangle is bounded by the SCM, the midline and the mandible, and is divided by the digastric and omohyoid muscles into submandibular, submental, carotid and muscular triangles. The posterior triangle is bounded by SCM, trapezius and the clavicle. It contains the accessory nerve (CN XI) running superficially, the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus, the third part of the subclavian artery and the external jugular vein. The accessory nerve lies superficially, and lymph node biopsy here can injure it, causing a weak shrug and shoulder droop. Erb point, the midpoint of the posterior border of SCM, is where the lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves emerge, and is the site of cervical plexus blocks.

The carotid sheath contains the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve. The common carotid bifurcates at about the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4) into the internal carotid, which has no branches in the neck, and the external carotid, which gives superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary and superficial temporal arteries. The carotid sinus (a baroreceptor, CN IX) and carotid body (a chemoreceptor, CN IX) lie at the bifurcation. Carotid endarterectomy exposes the bifurcation along the anterior border of SCM, with risk to the hypoglossal and vagus nerves.

The thyroid gland has two lobes joined by an isthmus lying anterior to the second to fourth tracheal rings. It is supplied by the superior thyroid artery (from the external carotid) and inferior thyroid artery (from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian). The superior laryngeal nerve, particularly its external branch which supplies the cricothyroid muscle, lies near the superior thyroid artery, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve is near the inferior thyroid artery; each is at risk during thyroidectomy, causing voice weakness or hoarseness respectively. The parathyroid glands, normally four, lie on the posterior surface and may be damaged, causing hypocalcaemia. The thyroid develops from the foramen caecum and descends along the thyroglossal duct, so a thyroglossal duct cyst lies in the midline and moves upward with tongue protrusion.

Cervical fascia creates spaces through which infection travels. The retropharyngeal space lies behind the pharynx and in front of the prevertebral fascia and communicates with the posterior mediastinum, so a retropharyngeal abscess can spread to the chest. Ludwig angina is a bilateral submandibular space infection, usually odontogenic from the mandibular molars, that can elevate the tongue and obstruct the airway. Emergency airway access is by cricothyrotomy through the cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, which is superficial and avascular relative to a tracheotomy.

lessons.title: Face, Orbit and Oral Region
body: Sensation of the face is supplied by the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve: V1 to the forehead, upper eyelid and nose bridge, V2 to the cheek, upper lip and lower eyelid, and V3 to the lower lip, chin and lower jaw (apart from the angle of the mandible, supplied by C2-C3). The muscles of facial expression are supplied by branches of the facial nerve, which fans out from within the parotid gland as temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches. The parotid gland is enclosed by a tight fascia and has an important surgical relationship: the facial nerve runs through it, so parotid surgery risks facial palsy. Stensen duct crosses the masseter and pierces the buccinator to open opposite the upper second molar. Parotid swelling in mumps is painful because the capsule is unyielding, and the auriculotemporal nerve carries the pain.

The orbit has a roof, floor, medial and lateral walls with several openings. The optic canal in the sphenoid transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery. The superior orbital fissure transmits CN III, IV, V1 and VI and the superior ophthalmic vein; the inferior orbital fissure transmits the maxillary branch to the infraorbital nerve. The weakest wall is the floor (and medial wall, thin as lamina papyracea). A blow to the eye can cause a blowout fracture of the floor, in which the orbital contents herniate into the maxillary sinus; the inferior rectus muscle can become entrapped, so the patient cannot look up and has diplopia, and infraorbital nerve injury causes numbness of the cheek and upper lip.

The lacrimal gland, supplied by parasympathetic fibres from the facial nerve (via the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion), drains through the lacrimal puncta to the nasolacrimal duct and inferior meatus of the nose. Sympathetic fibres from the superior cervical ganglion dilate the pupil and raise the eyelid by Muller muscle. Interruption of the sympathetic chain gives Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis. The parasympathetic pupil path is by the Edinger-Westphal nucleus to CN III, the ciliary ganglion and the sphincter pupillae.

The tongue has taste and general sensation to the anterior two thirds by the chorda tympani (taste) and the lingual nerve (touch, a branch of V3), and the posterior third by IX. Intrinsic and extrinsic muscles are supplied by XII, except palatoglossus, supplied by X. Lymph from the tongue tip drains to the submental nodes, and the lateral tongue to submandibular nodes, which matters in oral cancer staging. The inferior alveolar nerve block anaesthetises the lower teeth by injection near the mandibular foramen, and the nearby lingual nerve is usually anaesthetised at the same time.

lessons.title: Surface Anatomy and Clinical Landmarks
body: Surface anatomy links what a clinician can feel to what lies beneath. Good landmarks are bony and reliable. The suprasternal notch lies at about T2-T3, the sternal angle at T4-T5, the xiphisternal joint at about T9, and the inferior costal margin at about L2-L3 (the tenth costal cartilage). In the neck the hyoid sits at C3, the thyroid cartilage at C4-C5 and the cricoid cartilage at C6, which marks the junction of the larynx and trachea, the pharynx and oesophagus, and the level where the carotid artery can be compressed against the C6 transverse process (the carotid tubercle). The spinous process of C7 (vertebra prominens) is the prominent one at the base of the neck.

The transpyloric plane (of Addison) lies midway between the suprasternal notch and the pubic symphysis, at about L1. It passes through the pylorus, the neck of the pancreas, the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, the hila of the kidneys, the duodenojejunal flexure, the fundus of the gallbladder at the tip of the ninth costal cartilage, and the termination of the spinal cord. The subcostal plane is at L3, the supracristal plane at L4 (the level of aortic bifurcation and lumbar puncture) and the intertubercular plane at L5 across the iliac tubercles, where the inferior vena cava forms. The scapular spine lies at T3 and the inferior angle of the scapula at T7. Dermatomes provide a further map: T4 at the nipple, T10 at the umbilicus and L1 at the inguinal ligament.

Cardiac and lung borders also map to the surface. The apex beat is normally in the fifth left intercostal space at the midclavicular line. The lungs reach the sixth rib at the midclavicular line, the eighth in the midaxillary line and the tenth posteriorly, whereas the pleura extends two ribs lower: the eighth, tenth and twelfth, respectively. The oblique fissures follow a line from the T3 spine to the sixth costochondral junction, which helps decide where to auscultate each lobe. The right horizontal fissure follows the fourth rib anteriorly.

In the limbs, palpation sites matter: the carotid pulse at the anterior border of SCM at C6, the brachial pulse medial to the biceps tendon, the radial pulse lateral to flexor carpi radialis, the femoral pulse at the midinguinal point, the popliteal pulse deep in the fossa, the dorsalis pedis lateral to extensor hallucis longus and the posterior tibial pulse behind the medial malleolus. The ulnar nerve is palpable behind the medial epicondyle and the common fibular nerve against the neck of the fibula. A worked example: a stab wound at the left fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line is likely to enter the left ventricle, because the apex lies there and the lung and pleura retract at that level.

lessons.title: Embryologic Origins That Explain Anatomy
body: Many adult relationships make sense only through development. The pharyngeal arches give the head and neck their nerves and muscles. Arch 1 is supplied by the trigeminal nerve (V3 for the muscles of mastication), arch 2 by the facial nerve (muscles of facial expression, stapedius), arch 3 by the glossopharyngeal nerve (stylopharyngeus only), arches 4 and 6 by the vagus (laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles). The recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the sixth arch artery on the left (the ductus arteriosus) and under the fourth arch artery on the right (the right subclavian artery), which explains the left-right asymmetry. Pharyngeal pouches give the middle ear and tubes (1), palatine tonsil (2), inferior parathyroids and thymus (3) and superior parathyroids (4). A lateral neck cyst along the anterior border of SCM is a branchial cleft cyst from the second arch region.

The diaphragm forms from the septum transversum (central tendon), pleuroperitoneal membranes, oesophageal mesentery and body-wall muscle. The septum transversum arises at cervical levels, so the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) travels from the neck to the diaphragm. A congenital diaphragmatic hernia, most often through the posterolateral foramen of Bochdalek on the left, allows abdominal contents into the chest, compresses the developing lung and causes pulmonary hypoplasia.

The midgut herniates into the umbilical cord at week 6 and returns by week 10, rotating 270 degrees counterclockwise around the SMA, so a failure leads to malrotation, volvulus and obstruction. Persistence of the vitelline duct gives Meckel diverticulum. The foregut rotation moves the stomach so the left vagus becomes anterior; the dorsal mesentery of the foregut and the rotation also create the lesser sac. The heart tube loops to the right; the atrial septum (septum primum and secundum, with the foramen ovale) closes at birth when left atrial pressure rises, and a patent foramen ovale may allow paradoxical embolism. A ventricular septal defect is the most common congenital heart anomaly and usually involves the membranous septum.

The urogenital system also tells a story. The kidneys develop from the pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros; the metanephros ascends from the pelvis. A horseshoe kidney becomes trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent. The gonads descend from the posterior abdominal wall via the gubernaculum, and testicular lymph drains to para-aortic nodes for this reason. A patent processus vaginalis permits an indirect hernia or hydrocele. In males, the paramesonephric ducts regress under anti-Mullerian hormone; in females the same ducts form the uterine tubes, uterus and upper vagina. The ureteric bud arises from the mesonephric duct, and duplications of the ureter can result when two buds develop.

lessons.title: Imaging Anatomy: Radiograph, CT, MRI and Ultrasound
body: Each imaging modality maps tissue properties onto grey levels, so you must know what the picture represents. A plain radiograph is a shadow summing all tissues along the X-ray path: bone and calcium appear white because they attenuate strongly, air black, with fat and soft tissue in between. Overlying structures can hide each other, which is why two views at right angles are usually needed. In a posteroanterior chest film the heart normally occupies less than half of the maximum internal chest width, the right heart border is formed by the right atrium, and the left heart border by the left ventricle and the left atrial appendage, with the aortic knuckle (arch) above. A blunted costophrenic angle suggests a pleural effusion, since fluid pools in the costodiaphragmatic recess. The silhouette sign is the loss of an expected border when an adjacent structure has the same density: loss of the right heart border suggests right middle lobe disease.

Computed tomography (CT) acquires cross-sectional slices from X-ray attenuation, expressed in Hounsfield units (water is 0, air about minus 1000, dense bone strongly positive). It excels at bone, lung, acute haemorrhage (blood is bright) and rapid trauma assessment. Intravenous iodinated contrast enhances vessels and organs. Axial images are viewed as if looking up from the patient's feet, so the patient's right is on the viewer's left. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses the behaviour of hydrogen nuclei in a magnetic field. On T1-weighted images fat is bright and fluid dark, giving good anatomical detail; on T2-weighted images fluid is bright, which makes oedema and many lesions conspicuous. MRI offers excellent soft tissue contrast of the brain, spinal cord, joints and pelvis, with no ionising radiation, but takes longer and is contraindicated with some implants.

Ultrasound uses reflected sound and is real-time, portable and free of radiation. Fluid appears black (anechoic), which makes it suited to the gallbladder, kidneys, pregnancy and the heart, while bone and air reflect sound and obscure deeper structures. Doppler imaging measures flow. Choosing a test therefore follows the anatomy: a suspected pleural effusion on ultrasound or chest film, an acute head bleed on CT, a torn cruciate ligament or spinal cord lesion on MRI, a free-air perforation on an upright chest film or CT.

A systematic approach prevents missed findings: confirm the patient and the side, check technique and orientation, review the structures from the outside inward (soft tissue, bones, pleura and lungs, mediastinum), and compare both sides. Anatomical knowledge underpins interpretation. For example, on an axial CT of the upper abdomen at the level of the pancreas, the splenic vein runs behind the body of the pancreas, the aorta lies in front of the vertebral body slightly left of midline and the IVC to its right, so one can identify each structure by position, not by guessing.
